title: Sum of Digits (Digital Root)
directAnswer: Extract digits with repeated % 10 and / 10 to get the one-pass sum. If the prompt wants the *repeated* sum until a single digit (the digital root), you can loop the digit-sum until n < 10 — or skip the loop entirely with the O(1) congruence formula: dr(n) = 1 + (n − 1) % 9 for n > 0.

remember.pattern: Digit extraction via %10 // 10, plus the mod-9 digital-root shortcut
remember.formula:
# one-pass digit sum
s = 0
while n > 0:
    s += n % 10
    n //= 10

# digital root in O(1)
dr = 0 if n == 0 else 1 + (n - 1) % 9
rules: `n % 10` peels off the **last** digit; `n //= 10` drops it. Forgetting the `//= 10` is an infinite loop.
The digital root is **not** `n % 9`. That formula returns `0` for multiples of 9 (like 18 → 0) when the true root is `9`. Use `1 + (n − 1) % 9`.
Handle `n = 0` separately: its digit sum and digital root are both `0`, but `1 + (n − 1) % 9` would give the wrong answer.
Take `abs(n)` first if negatives are allowed — `−123 % 10` differs by language (Java gives `−3`, Python gives `7`).
Be clear which problem you're solving: a *single* pass (sum the digits once) versus *repeated* summing down to one digit (the digital root).
whenToUse: You need to collapse a number to a single-digit fingerprint (checksums, Harshad/Niven checks)
Validating IDs/card numbers where a digit-derived check value is required
Any time you'd otherwise convert to a string just to add digits — the arithmetic version is cleaner
The repeated-sum / digital-root framing where the O(1) congruence is the standout answer
antiSignals: You need the digits in order or by position → string/array indexing is clearer than %10 //10
You need digits of an arbitrary-precision BigInteger → string traversal avoids slow big-number divides
The number is given as a string already → just iterate characters
remember.takeaway: The loop is trivial; the interview edge is the digital-root insight — that repeatedly summing digits is congruent to n mod 9, so the whole repeated process collapses to one O(1) formula once you guard 0 and multiples of 9.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you extract digits with clean modular arithmetic instead of string conversion, and whether you know the digital root has a closed form rather than needing a nested loop.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Writing `n % 9` for the digital root (wrong for multiples of 9 and for 0), or forgetting the `n //= 10` and spinning forever.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Solve the literal sum in one pass, then volunteer that the *repeated* sum equals the digital root and reduces to `1 + (n − 1) % 9` in O(1) — and explain *why* via casting out nines.

problemStatement:
Given a non-negative integer `n`, return the sum of its digits.

Clarify whether the interviewer wants a **single** pass (e.g. `38 → 3 + 8 = 11`) or the **repeated** digit sum until one digit remains — the *digital root* (e.g. `38 → 11 → 2`).
constraints: n fits in a 64-bit integer; for larger inputs treat n as a string
If negatives are permitted, operate on |n|
understanding: Peel digits off the right end with %10, accumulate them, and shift right with integer division. The 'repeated' variant keeps collapsing the sum until a single digit remains, which has a neat mod-9 closed form.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Single pass or repeated until one digit?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: This changes the whole answer. Single pass is a plain loop; repeated is the digital root, which has an O(1) formula.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can n be negative?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: If so I take the absolute value first, because the sign of `%` differs between Java and Python and would corrupt the sum.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large can n be?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: If it can exceed a 64-bit integer, I treat the input as a string and add each character's digit — arithmetic divides on big numbers are slower.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What should n = 0 return?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Zero, for both the simple sum and the digital root. I special-case it because the closed-form formula assumes n > 0.

examples.explanation: 18 → 9. Note 18 % 9 = 0, which is why the naive `n % 9` formula is wrong — the answer is 9, not 0.

diagrams.title: Which digit problem are you solving?

approaches.name: One-Pass Digit Extraction (Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: The default answer for the literal 'sum the digits' prompt and the building block for the repeated version.
hints: How do you get the last digit of a number without converting it to text? Think about the remainder when you divide by 10.
`n % 10` is the last digit; `n / 10` (integer division) removes it. Loop until n becomes 0.
Accumulate `n % 10` into a sum, then assign `n = n / 10` each iteration. The loop runs once per digit.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A number with d digits satisfies d ≈ log₁₀(n) + 1, and the loop runs once per digit, so the work is O(log n). Only a single accumulator is stored.
approaches.explanation:
Repeatedly take the last digit with `n % 10`, add it to a running sum, then strip that digit with integer division `n /= 10`. Stop when `n` reaches `0`.

**Why modulo and integer division are the right tools.** Base-10 positional notation means the last digit *is* the remainder modulo 10, and dividing by 10 (discarding the remainder) shifts every digit one place right — exactly like deleting the last character of the number. Two cheap arithmetic ops give you digit access without ever allocating a string.

**Why the loop must update n.** The terminating condition is `n > 0`, and the only thing that drives `n` toward `0` is the `n /= 10`. Drop that line and `n` never changes, so the loop spins forever — the single most common bug on this problem. Always pair the `% 10` read with the `/= 10` shrink.

**Why you should take the absolute value for negatives.** In Java, `-123 % 10` is `-3`; in Python it's `7`. Either way you don't want signed remainders polluting a digit sum, so normalize with `abs(n)` up front when the spec allows negatives.

**Why string conversion is usually worse here.** Converting to a string and summing `int(ch)` works and reads fine, but it allocates, and the arithmetic version is the one interviewers expect because it shows you can manipulate numbers directly. Reach for the string only when the value is arbitrary-precision and big-number division would be slow.
approaches.insight: `% 10` and `/= 10` are the universal 'read the last digit, then drop it' pair. Internalize them and a whole family of problems — palindrome number, reverse integer, Armstrong number — uses the exact same two lines.

dryRun.intro: Peel the last digit with %10, add it, then shift right with //10.

code.python:
def sum_of_digits(self, n: int) -> int:
    n = abs(n)
    total = 0
    while n > 0:
        total += n % 10   # last digit
        n //= 10          # drop it
    return total

java.explanation: Normalize sign so a negative remainder can't corrupt the sum.
n % 10 is the rightmost digit in base 10.
Integer division shifts every digit right — this is what drives the loop to 0. Omit it and you loop forever.

python.explanation: Python's % on negatives returns a positive remainder, but abs keeps behavior consistent with the math.
Floor division drops the last digit; without it the while loop never terminates.

diagrams.title: Digits peeled right-to-left
diagrams.caption: Each frame strips one digit off the right and adds it to the sum.

pitfalls: Not taking abs(n) when negatives are allowed — signed remainders break the sum.
Converting to a string when the arithmetic version is cleaner and allocation-free.

approaches.name: Digital Root in O(1) (Optimal for the repeated sum)
approaches.whenToMention: When the prompt asks for the *repeated* digit sum until one digit remains — replace the nested loop with one congruence.
hints: Repeatedly summing digits preserves the value modulo 9 — adding digits is 'casting out nines'. Why might that be?
Every power of 10 is congruent to 1 mod 9 (10 ≡ 1, 100 ≡ 1, …), so a number equals the sum of its digits mod 9.
The single-digit result is therefore n mod 9 — except multiples of 9 map to 9, not 0, and n = 0 maps to 0. The clean closed form is `1 + (n − 1) % 9` for n > 0.
approaches.complexityReasoning: No loop at all — a constant number of arithmetic operations regardless of how many digits n has.
approaches.explanation:
The *repeated* digit sum (keep summing until one digit remains) is called the **digital root**, and it equals `n` reduced modulo 9 — with two careful adjustments. So the entire nested process collapses into a single formula evaluated in constant time.

**Why the digit sum is congruent to n mod 9.** Write `n` in base 10: `n = d_k·10^k + … + d_1·10 + d_0`. Since `10 ≡ 1 (mod 9)`, every power `10^i ≡ 1 (mod 9)`, so `n ≡ d_k + … + d_1 + d_0 (mod 9)` — the number and its digit sum leave the *same* remainder when divided by 9. This is the old 'casting out nines' trick. Repeating the digit sum never changes that remainder, so the final single digit is just `n mod 9`.

**Why plain `n % 9` is wrong.** The catch is the boundary. For a positive multiple of 9 (like 18 or 99), `n % 9 == 0`, but the digital root is `9`, not `0`. And `n = 0` genuinely has digital root `0`. The expression `1 + (n − 1) % 9` threads both needles: for `n = 9` it gives `1 + 8 % 9 = 9`; for `n = 18` it gives `1 + 17 % 9 = 9`; for `n = 10` it gives `1 + 9 % 9 = 1`. You still special-case `n = 0` because `(0 − 1) % 9` is not what we want.

**Why this is the standout answer.** Most candidates write a `while n >= 10` loop that calls the digit-sum repeatedly — correct, but O(log n) per pass and visibly more code. Producing the closed form and *explaining the mod-9 reason* signals genuine number-theory fluency rather than pattern matching.

**When to still loop.** If the interviewer wants to *see* the intermediate sums (e.g. for a teaching demo), or the base isn't 10, the loop is the safer, more transparent choice.
approaches.insight: Repeated digit summing is a mod-9 operation in disguise. Recognizing that an apparently iterative process has an algebraic closed form — and guarding the two boundary cases — is the whole trick.

dryRun.intro: Skip the nested loop: digital root = 1 + (n − 1) % 9 for n > 0.

java.explanation: Special case: the formula assumes n > 0, but 0's digital root is genuinely 0.
Maps multiples of 9 to 9 (not 0) and everything else to its 1..9 digital root.

python.explanation: Guard before applying the closed form.
Casting-out-nines congruence, shifted to land 9 instead of 0 on multiples of 9.

diagrams.title: Why repeated summing equals n mod 9
diagrams.caption: Each power of 10 is congruent to 1 mod 9, so the digit sum keeps the same remainder.

edgeCases.behavior: Special-cased to return 0; the formula would otherwise mishandle (0 − 1) % 9.
1 + (18 − 1) % 9 = 1 + 8 = 9 — the multiple-of-9 case the naive n % 9 gets wrong.

pitfalls: Writing `n % 9` directly — returns 0 for multiples of 9 instead of 9.
Applying the formula to n = 0 without the guard.
Forgetting abs(n) so a negative input feeds the formula a negative remainder.

commonMistakes: Using `n % 9` as the digital root — wrong for multiples of 9 and for 0.
Omitting the `n /= 10` shift, causing an infinite loop.
Not normalizing negative inputs with abs(n) before taking remainders.
Confusing the single-pass sum with the repeated digital root.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Using n % 9 for the digital root
commonMistakesDetailed.why: For positive multiples of 9 the remainder is 0, but the true digital root is 9. The shifted formula fixes the boundary.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Infinite loop from a missing shift
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you read n % 10 but never divide n by 10, n stays the same and the while condition never becomes false.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
total = 0
while n > 0:
    total += n % 10
    # forgot n //= 10 — loops forever
return total
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
total = 0
while n > 0:
    total += n % 10
    n //= 10
return total

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Signed remainder on negative input
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Java's `-123 % 10` is -3, so summing without abs() yields a smaller (or negative) total than intended.
